name: Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injury
summary: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is a strong band inside the knee that stops the shin bone (tibia) from sliding too far forward under the thigh bone (femur) and helps control twisting. An ACL injury is usually a sprain or a tear.

looksLike: Sudden twisting, landing or deceleration injury, often with a pop or tearing feeling.
Immediate or rapid swelling within hours, which suggests bleeding inside the joint (haemarthrosis).
Inability to continue activity, pain, and a feeling of the knee giving way.
Difficulty fully straightening or bending the knee because of swelling and pain.
Associated injuries are common: meniscal tears, medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury, bone bruising.
redFlags: Gross instability in several directions, severe swelling, history of a high-energy injury
Foot drop or numbness over the outer lower leg and top of foot
Inability to bear weight, bony tenderness, deformity
Hot red knee with fever after injury or surgery

Justifying findings: mechanism, swelling, positive Lachman or pivot shift.

assess: Observe swelling, bruising, gait and muscle bulk.
Assess for effusion, and record range of movement. Note any loss of full extension.
Palpate joint lines, MCL, patella and the head of the fibula.

blocks.text: The **anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)** is a strong band inside the knee that stops the shin bone (tibia) from sliding too far forward under the thigh bone (femur) and helps control twisting. An ACL injury is usually a sprain or a tear. It is most common in pivoting and landing sports such as football, basketball, netball and skiing [Ref - to verify]. Most ACL injuries happen without contact, for example when a player lands, cuts or side-steps. Contact injuries also occur.

A torn ACL does not heal by itself in the usual sense. Treatment options are structured rehabilitation with or without later reconstruction surgery. Both can lead to good results in selected patients, and the choice depends on instability, sport and work demands, associated injuries and patient preference [Ref - to verify].

items: Sudden twisting, landing or deceleration injury, often with a pop or tearing feeling.
Immediate or rapid swelling within hours, which suggests bleeding inside the joint (haemarthrosis).
Inability to continue activity, pain, and a feeling of the knee giving way.
Difficulty fully straightening or bending the knee because of swelling and pain.
Associated injuries are common: meniscal tears, medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury, bone bruising.

blocks.text: Honest note: the accuracy of ACL tests is higher when the patient is relaxed, so tests may be easier after the acute pain has settled. Compare with the uninjured knee every time [Ref - to verify].
E1. Lachman test (preferred first test)

rows: Check for increased forward movement of the tibia on the femur
Supine, leg relaxed, knee bent about 20 to 30 degrees
Beside the knee being tested; one hand stabilises the lower thigh, the other holds the upper shin behind the tibial head
With the thigh held still, pull the tibia forward in a smooth, firm movement. Feel the amount of movement and the quality of the end-point. Repeat on the other knee
More forward movement than the uninjured knee, with a soft or absent end-point
Similar movement to the other knee, with a firm end-point

A negative result does not fully exclude a tear, especially in acute injury with guarding or a large effusion, or with some partial tears [Ref - to verify]. Large hands or a large thigh can make the test hard
Knee bent too far; the thigh not stabilised; hamstring contraction; the foot not relaxed
If positive, check associated injuries and arrange medical review and imaging

blocks.text: E2. Anterior drawer test

rows: Supine, hip bent to 45 degrees, knee bent to 90 degrees, foot flat on the bed
Sit lightly on the foot to hold it, hold the upper shin with both hands, and pull the tibia forward
Increased forward movement compared with the other knee
Less sensitive than the Lachman test, especially in acute injury, because hamstring guarding and swelling limit it [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E3. Pivot shift test

rows: Reproduce the rotational instability of an ACL-deficient knee
Supine, leg relaxed, hip slightly flexed
Hold the foot and shin, apply an inward rotation to the shin and a valgus stress while moving the knee from extension into flexion
A sudden shift or clunk as the tibia reduces, usually at about 20 to 40 degrees of flexion
Very specific when positive, but hard to perform in an awake, guarded patient; not often possible in the acute stage [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E4. Associated injury checks

rows: Increased opening compared with the other knee; pain
Backward shift or sag of the tibia

blocks.text: E5. Imaging
MRI is ordered by a doctor to confirm the tear and show associated injuries. X-rays are used to exclude fractures, and a decision rule such as the Ottawa knee rules may be used [Ref - to verify].

rows: Joint-line pain, locking, catching, delayed swelling
Fall onto the front of the shin, posterior sag
Inability to bear weight, bony tenderness
Gross instability, possible vessel and nerve injury

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Gross instability in several directions, severe swelling, history of a high-energy injury
Multiligament injury or knee dislocation, possibly with vessel injury
Check foot pulses and colour; call emergency services if abnormal
Foot drop or numbness over the outer lower leg and top of foot
Inability to bear weight, bony tenderness, deformity
Hot red knee with fever after injury or surgery

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Mechanism, rapid swelling and a positive Lachman or pivot shift? **Yes:** working diagnosis is suspected ACL tear. Refer for imaging and orthopaedic opinion, and begin early rehabilitation.

Decide with the patient and surgeon between rehabilitation first and reconstruction. Factors that favour early surgery include a young athlete returning to pivoting sports, repeated giving way, a repairable meniscal tear or multiligament injury [Ref - to verify].
A rehabilitation-first approach is reasonable for many patients, including those with lower demands, with surgery later if instability continues [Ref - to verify].

rows: Prevent stiffness, support extension and flexion
Reduced patellar glide after injury or surgery
Persistent loss of extension or flexion

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** early active rehabilitation. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Do not use techniques that force anterior tibial translation. Avoid aggressive stretching into a swollen knee.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** progress by criteria, not by weeks. Early goals are controlling swelling, regaining full extension and quadriceps activation. Later goals are strength, landing control, running readiness and sport-specific work [Ref - to verify].

rows: Heel slides, passive extension holds, quadriceps sets, straight leg raise, walking with aids as needed, ankle pumps
Reduce swelling, regain full extension and flexion, activate the quadriceps
Minimal swelling, full extension, good quadriceps control
Sit-to-stand, mini-squats, leg press, step-ups, hip and calf strengthening, stationary bike
Pain and swelling stay low; strength improving
Single-leg balance, single-leg squats, deceleration drills, walk-to-run progression
No swelling after loading, good control, adequate strength
Cutting, jumping, change-of-direction drills, sport drills

blocks.text: **Quadriceps strengthening:** closed-chain and open-chain knee extension are both used, and loads and ranges are adjusted to avoid pain and strain on the graft after surgery [Ref - to verify].

**Return to sport criteria (example):** near-normal strength (often 90 percent or more of the other leg), hop test performance of 90 percent or more of the other leg, no swelling or giving way, good movement quality, and psychological readiness assessed with a tool such as the ACL-RSI. Many programs delay return to pivoting sport until about 9 months or longer after reconstruction, because returning earlier has been linked with higher re-injury risk [Ref - to verify]. No fixed date is set here.
**Injury prevention:** neuromuscular training (strength, landing technique, balance) reduces ACL injury risk in sport [Ref - to verify].

rows: Possible when voluntary quadriceps activation is poor
May help early activation [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: After surgery, follow the surgeon's protocol for bracing, weight-bearing and range limits.

blocks.text: **Case:** A 19-year-old footballer felt a pop while landing and fell. The knee swelled within 2 hours. He cannot fully straighten it. Lachman shows more forward movement than the other knee with a soft end-point. Valgus stress is normal. Pulses and sensation are normal. He wants to return to football.

**Working diagnosis:** suspected ACL tear. **Plan:** exclude fracture through a doctor, control swelling, restore full extension and quadriceps activation, MRI and orthopaedic opinion, discuss reconstruction versus rehabilitation in view of his sport, begin criteria-based rehabilitation.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why is the Lachman test preferred over the anterior drawer? It is usually more sensitive and easier to perform in a painful, guarded knee [Ref - to verify].
Why check pulses and sensation? A knee dislocation or severe ligament injury can damage vessels and nerves, which is an emergency.
Why is regaining full extension so important early? Loss of extension can cause lasting walking and strength problems and makes later recovery harder [Ref - to verify].
Why not rely on a fixed number of months for return to sport? Strength, control and confidence vary between people. Returning too early is linked to re-injury, so criteria matter [Ref - to verify].
The patient has an unstable knee that keeps giving way despite good rehabilitation. What next? Discuss reconstruction with the surgeon because repeated giving way risks further injury to the knee.
**Initial approach:** safety screen, swelling control, extension and quadriceps activation.
**Justifying findings:** mechanism, swelling, positive Lachman or pivot shift.
**Priority:** a clear decision about rehabilitation first or surgery, with a criteria-based plan.
**Manual therapy:** minor adjunct.
**Exercise:** staged strengthening, landing control, running and sport drills.
**Modalities:** limited role; NMES selected.
**Tell the patient:** many people return to sport but it takes time; both pathways are options.
**Avoid:** forcing tests in an acute knee, early return to pivoting sport, ignoring associated injuries.
**Measure:** swelling, range, strength, hop tests, KOOS or IKDC, ACL-RSI.
**If no improvement:** specialist review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** return-to-sport criteria met and a prevention program in place.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** isolated ACL injury, no fracture, no neurovascular injury.

items: **Can be tested:** outcomes of rehabilitation first versus early reconstruction; which return-to-sport criteria best predict re-injury.
**Hypotheses:** that neuromuscular training reduces injury risk by improving landing mechanics.
**Future questions:** best graft and rehabilitation program; how to lower long-term osteoarthritis risk.
